## Explicit vs. Implicit Formulations

Academic libraries show a structural divide in how they formalize AI literacy. Across the corpus, **45.5% (*n* = 5)** provide explicit, formal definitions of "AI Literacy," while **54.5% (*n* = 6)** operationalize the concept implicitly through distributed heuristics, competency checklists, and policy frameworks.

```
+-------------------+-----------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| INSTITUTION       | DEFINITION STATUS           | PRIMARY CONCEPTUAL MODEL                                    |
+-------------------+-----------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Auburn            | Explicit Definition         | Functional-Ethical Triad (Functions, Ethics, Application)   |
| Baylor            | Implicit Characterization   | Computational Research Integration                          |
| Chapman           | Explicit Definition         | Sociotechnical Habits of Mind / Cognitive Preservation      |
| UArkansas         | Implicit Characterization   | Vendor Discovery & Provenance Mechanics                     |
| UC Davis          | Implicit Characterization   | Collaborative Technical-Integrity Schema (CLEAR / ROBOT)   |
| UC Irvine         | Implicit Characterization   | Critical Information Literacy (CIL) & ACRL Alignment        |
| UC Merced         | Implicit Characterization   | Workflow-Institutional Compliance Integration               |
| UC Santa Barbara  | Explicit Definition         | Three-Stage Developmental Model (Understand-Apply-Evaluate) |
| UC San Diego      | Implicit Characterization   | Structured Prompting & Academic Integrity Safeguards        |
| USC               | Explicit Definition         | Leo S. Lo Multidimensional Taxonomy                         |
| William & Mary    | Explicit Definition         | Demystified Foundational Literacy & Evaluative Due Diligence|
+-------------------+-----------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## Prominent Conceptual Models

### 1. Leo S. Lo’s Multidimensional Framework (USC & Chapman)

**USC** and **Chapman** explicitly adopt or adapt the framework developed by Leo S. Lo (2025), defining AI literacy as an ecosystemic competency:

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
> *"AI literacy goes beyond understanding AI tools; it equips individuals to critically evaluate, ethically navigate, and practically apply AI in real-world scenarios; [it is] the ability to understand, use, and think critically about AI technologies and their impact on society, ethics, and everyday life."*
> — **USC Libraries & Chapman University LibGuides**
:::

This model establishes four interconnected pillars:
- **Technical Mechanics**: Understanding how probabilistic models generate outputs.
- **Practical Application**: Formulating structured prompts and integrating tools effectively.
- **Critical Evaluation**: Auditing for hallucination, bias, and epistemic gaps.
- **Socio-Ethical Navigation**: Navigating copyright, privacy, labor, and environmental costs.

---

### 2. Developmental Stages of Literacy (UC Santa Barbara)

**UC Santa Barbara (UCSB)** operationalizes AI literacy through a developmental continuum modeled directly on foundational reading and writing acquisition:

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
> *"The practice of learning how to identify, use, and evaluate AI tools and products is building a set of literacies similar to when a person learns to read, write, and think critically."*
> — **UCSB Library**
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "UCSB Three-Stage Developmental AI Literacy Model"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '14px'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    A["`Stage 1: Understand AI    
    Mechanics, Machine Learning, NLP`"]
    B["`Stage 2: Use and Apply AI
    Prompting, Research, Synthesis, Coding`"]
    C["`Stage 3: Analyze and Evaluate AI
        Hallucinations, Ethics, IP, Bias`"]
    
    A --> B
    B --> C
```

---

### 3. Cognitive Habits of Mind & Demystification (Chapman & William & Mary)

**Chapman University** centers its definition around cognitive habits and human metacognition:

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
> *"AI doesn't damage our brains, but unthinking use can damage our thinking. What's at stake isn't our neurons but our habits of mind."*
> — **Chapman University LibGuide**
:::

**William & Mary** explicitly demystifies technical gatekeeping, decoupling AI literacy from advanced computer science requirements:

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
> *"Being AI Literate does not mean you need to understand the advanced mechanics of AI... you don't need to be a data scientist, programmer, or application developer... However, you do need to have a basic understanding of what artificial intelligence is, what it isn't, how it works, and how to use it ethically and legally."*
> — **William & Mary Libraries**
:::

---

## Intersecting AI Literacy with Information and Digital Literacies

Across all surveyed institutions, AI literacy is conceptualized not as a detached, isolated domain, but as an advanced evolution of **Information Literacy** and **Digital Literacy**:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Convergence of Digital, Information, and AI Literacies"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '14px'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    DL["`Digital Literacy
         Computational tools, data structures, campus IT security`"]
    IL["`Information Literacy
         Authority is constructed, source evaluation, attribution ethics`"]
    AL["`AI Literacy
    Probabilistic output appraisal, prompt engineering, sociotechnical ethics`"]

    DL --> IL
    IL --> AL
```

- **Digital Literacy** provides the infrastructural baseline: understanding campus data security tiers (e.g. UC Merced P2/P4 classifications), compute environments, and API endpoints.
- **Information Literacy** provides the epistemic anchor: as UC Irvine notes, *"The question of whether you can trust a chatbot's output is fundamentally a question about information literacy."*
- **AI Literacy** synthesizes both to address non-deterministic outputs, non-reproducible research summaries (UArkansas), algorithmic bias mitigation (UC Davis), and cognitive agency (Chapman).
